time.desc: The parties confirmed that a key security official was killed in an opponent's air strike, becoming one of the highest-ranking officials killed since the war began.

The coalition forces involved in the war launched air strikes on the opponent's giant natural gas fields in key sea areas and continued to attack its energy infrastructure. International oil prices rose in response.

One party participating in the war issued a time-limited ultimatum, requiring the reopening of commercial traffic on key energy waterways, otherwise it will attack the other party's power and other energy infrastructure.
The two sides confirmed that they had started dialogue, with one side announcing that it would suspend attacks on the other's energy facilities for several days to create a window for negotiations.
One party formally submitted a multi-clause plan to end the conflict, pushing the ceasefire negotiations into a text-based consultation stage.
The other side completed and submitted a formal response to the multi-clause plan, bringing the ceasefire negotiations to the next stage.
Major countries outside the region jointly proposed an alternative cessation framework, calling for an immediate ceasefire and the restoration of normal traffic on key waterways.

The leaders of one of the parties involved in the war publicly called on all countries to go to the key straits to rush to transport oil, claiming that the opponent had been basically defeated, and accused a neutral country of not cooperating.
Leaders of one side of the war announced in national addresses that they would crack down harder on their opponents in the coming weeks and once again set a timetable for ending the conflict.

Both sides in the conflict have publicly escalated threats and warnings of counterattacks against key waterways and infrastructure, including the option of a blockade that could extend to another strategic waterway.
One side agreed to suspend bombings and attacks against its opponents for about two weeks, forming a ceasefire window with a clear cutoff.
Allies publicly stated that the ceasefire did not cover their actions against third-party armed forces, sparking controversy over the scope and sustainability of the ceasefire.
Opponents proposed the idea of ​​charging tolls for passage through key straits, which was criticized as violating relevant treaties, and the game over passage rules continued.
One side's military officially launched a naval blockade against its opponent and stated that it would not affect the freedom of navigation of ships related to non-opponent ports.
